messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun, a 58‑year‑old South Asian man, spent his childhood watching his younger brother, Aamir, suffer from a severe bout of meningitis. The day he was pulled into the emergency department, the air was thick with antiseptic, the sight of a nurse’s white gloves, and the rhythmic thud of needles being inserted into Aamir’s veins. The memory captured that day in vivid, high‑resolution images—hospital corridors, white walls, a mother’s trembling hands. Years later, the mere smell of antiseptic at the clinic on his way to a routine check‑up can trigger that memory as if the air itself carried the old echo of the emergency room. He wakes in the middle of the night, heart racing, as if a phantom syringe might prick his arm. That immediate physical reactivity—his pulse surging, his palms sweating—amplifies his sense of vigilance; he feels he must stay alert to the next needle, the next beep. The experience also has seeded in him a harsh self‑label: he thinks of himself as weak because he was unable to protect his brother, and he fears that his uncontrollable reactions mean he is “going crazy.” These negative appraisals feed back into his vigilance: the belief that he cannot control the next crisis makes him hyper‑alert, and his fear of children—especially in a room full of laughing toddlers at a community event—stokes the same anxiety. Each trigger not only evokes the vivid visual memory of that hospital day but also re‑activates the threat of sudden illness, the negative emotions of fear and guilt, and the belief that he is a helpless, weak person. The memory, in turn, magnifies the threat; when the full sensory reliving of Aamir’s coughing in the ICU floods his mind, it feels as real as the current moment, and he feels that the same danger could erupt again. That same memory also feeds back into his appraisals: every time the smell of antiseptic reminds him of the loss, he cements the idea that he is fragile and doomed to repeat past failures. The cycle tightens as each element continually feeds the next—triggers spark memories, memories spark threat, threat amplifies negative appraisals, and appraisals generate new triggers. For the past twelve years, Arjun has worked as a bomb disposal technician, a job that demands sustained alertness and precision. The residual hyper‑vigilance that follows him into the workplace manifests as an almost constant mental checklist: “If there’s a pressure change, there’s a bomb.” After a particularly tense debriefing where a faulty alarm had almost gone off, he began avoiding any situation that might resemble a medical emergency. The hospital’s antiseptic scent lingered in the ventilation system of the disposal unit, and the sight of a syringe‑shaped drill bit in the field sent a shiver through him. Even in the calm of a routine inspection, his pulse would quicken, and he’d find himself pulling his jacket tighter, as if it could shield him from unseen needles. The fear that a child’s laughter might be a disguised threat has led him to decline invitations from his wife’s family, where children’s playrooms and birthday cakes often punctuate the environment. The isolation has strained his marriage; his wife, Laila, has noticed his reluctance to attend their daughter’s school play and has begged him to confront his anxiety. He has fallen asleep only after long periods of wakefulness, listening to the steady drumbeat of his heart, convinced that a sudden crisis is inevitable. The more he avoids triggers, the more his negative appraisals harden: he feels he cannot help himself, that the world is unsafe, and that he is a weak, helpless man who will never regain control. When Arjun finally agreed to a therapy appointment, it was after a night of insomnia that left him trembling in his own bed, hearing phantom needles in the dark. He was terrified that his own mind had become a battlefield, and he was hoping for a way to quiet the relentless inner alarms that kept him on edge even while he was in his own home. The most frightening thought that lingers is that he may never again feel safe in the presence of children or in the smell of antiseptic without being pulled back into the past. Yet he clings to the faint hope that, through understanding and training, he might reclaim a quiet, ordinary life with his wife and their children.
